label: Vehicle safety
title: A safer vehicle
headline: What's keeping you safe in your car?
intro: Many cars on Namibian roads are older imports. Learn which safety features matter most, and how to use the ones you have.

scenes.question: Electronic stability control (ESC) cuts the risk of a fatal single-vehicle crash in a car or SUV by about how much?

lines: You're buying a second-hand car. Two cars cost the same.
One is newer and has stability control and airbags. The other is older, with neither.

art.alt: A car with a safety shield symbol.

scenes.prompt: Rain on a bend, and you take it a little too fast. Compare a car with and without stability control.

art.alt: Top-down view of a wet bend, showing the path a car takes with and without stability control.

states.label: Without ESC
states.caption: Without ESC, the back of the car slides out and it runs wide, off the road or into the other lane.

states.label: With ESC
states.caption: ESC brakes single wheels in a split second and keeps the car on its line.

art.alt: Side view of a car with one safety feature highlighted at a time.

steps.title: Seatbelts
steps.body: Your first line of protection. Every seat, every trip.

steps.title: Airbags
steps.body: They work with your seatbelt, not instead of it.

steps.title: ABS brakes
steps.body: Let you keep steering while you brake hard.

steps.title: Stability control
steps.body: Stops skids before they start. Namibia doesn't require it, so check whether a car has it.

steps.title: Tyres
steps.body: The only part touching the road. The law requires a tread at least {claim:na.law.tread} deep across the whole tyre.

steps.title: Head restraints
steps.body: Set the top level with the top of your head to protect your neck.

scenes.explain: ESC cuts the risk of a fatal single-vehicle crash by about {claim:int.iihs.esc-single}, and of a fatal rollover in a car by {claim:int.iihs.esc-rollover}. Yet {claim:na.stat.esc-law}: Namibia has no law requiring it.

lines: Crash tests rate how well a car protects the people inside. Global NCAP's tests of cars sold in Africa have given some models {claim:int.gncap.africa} for adult protection.
Before you buy, look up the model's crash rating, and choose the safest car you can afford.

art.alt: Five rating stars, some filled and some empty.

lines: Choose the safest car you can afford: look up its crash rating first.
Check your tyres and lights regularly.
Safety features help, but you're still the one driving.

scenes.question: Wearing a seatbelt can cut the risk of death for people in a vehicle by up to how much?

lines: You're in the back of a friend's car for a short drive across town.
Nobody in the back is wearing a belt. It's only a few minutes.

art.alt: A car with a seatbelt symbol.

scenes.prompt: The car in front stops suddenly. Compare a crash-test dummy with and without a seatbelt.

art.alt: Side view of a crash-test dummy in a car seat during a sudden stop.

states.label: No belt
states.caption: Without a belt, the dummy keeps moving at the car's speed until it hits the seat, the dashboard or another person.

states.label: Belted
states.caption: The belt holds the dummy in its seat and spreads the force across the strong bones of the chest and hips.

scenes.explain: A seatbelt can cut the risk of death for people in a vehicle by up to {claim:int.who.seatbelt}. In Namibia every adult must wear one, in the front and the back.

questions.prompt: In Namibia, passengers in the back seat don't have to wear a seatbelt.
questions.reason: Every adult must wear a seatbelt in any seat that has one, front or back.

questions.prompt: It's legal to carry paying passengers in the back of a bakkie.
questions.reason: Nobody may carry people for payment in a goods compartment, such as a bakkie's load bin.

lines: Belt up in every seat, on every trip, however short.
As the driver, make sure everyone is belted before you move off.
Never ride on a load bin, the roof or a running board.
